purpose: what the original recovery fields meant, and what replaced them. The original CSVs, losses, parameter selections and simulation outputs are UNCHANGED; only the reporting is corrected.

true_would_be_finalist.original_meaning: the true (A, rho) cell had a screening rank <= 3, i.e. it WOULD have entered the finalists through the screen
true_would_be_finalist.what_it_was_wrongly_read_as: the truth was actually scored in the final re-check
true_would_be_finalist.why_that_is_wrong: the fixed baseline is appended to the candidate set whenever the screen does not already contain it, so in the A=1.0, rho=0.98 scenario the truth IS the baseline and was scored in every replicate regardless of its screening rank

replacement_fields.truth_in_screen_top3: unchanged in meaning, renamed so it cannot be misread
replacement_fields.truth_actually_scored_in_finalists: queried from market_recovery_finalists.csv: was a row with the true (A, rho) actually scored?

A1.0_rho0.98.note: the truth is the fixed baseline in this scenario

A1.4_rho0.96.note: the truth is not the baseline, so only the screen could admit it

training_loss.original_meaning: the final re-check loss of the SELECTED configuration on the pseudo-training returns
training_loss.added: training_loss_baseline, the same quantity for the fixed baseline, read from market_recovery_finalists.csv; and training_improvement = baseline - selected
training_loss.caveat: both are final-re-check numbers on 2000 paths. They contain the selection (the minimum over candidates is biased low) and the finite simulation error of that re-check; neither is a clean measure of fit quality.

withdrawn_statements: 'the parameters are unbiased' -- the mean selection error is -0.05 and -0.04 in A with a Monte-Carlo standard error of about 0.04 and 0.03 over 20 replicates. That is consistent with zero and does not establish unbiasedness.

'the procedure captured 70% of the available improvement' -- that was a ratio of two medians; the two paired means carry standard errors of 0.30 and 0.32, so their ratio is not a supportable point estimate.
'screening noise has been separately identified' -- this design varies the pseudo-history and the internal simulation together, so the two are not separated by it.

'selection noise is insufficient to explain the 2022 reversal' -- the two magnitudes come from different designs on different data and were never compared on a common footing; the comparison is withdrawn.

'the four versions share one evaluation stream, so a difference between them is not simulation noise' -- common random numbers REDUCE the noise of a paired comparison; they do not remove the finite simulation error, which is why each paired mean is reported with its own Monte-Carlo standard error.

'the chosen A spans a wide range while the evaluation losses stay narrow, so the distribution is stable and the parameters are unidentified' -- comparing the spread of a parameter with the spread of a loss does not establish either claim; the two are on different scales and neither spread was given a reference.

energy_score_definition.transform_and_standardisation: identical to J -- log for the three realised-volatility quantiles, raw for the five absolute-return autocorrelations, each divided by the same reference scale
energy_score_definition.weighting: NOT identical to J. J applies two groups of equal total weight, so each realised-volatility target carries 1/6 and each autocorrelation target 1/10. The energy score uses a plain Euclidean norm over the eight standardised components, i.e. 1/8 each.
energy_score_definition.scope: it evaluates the joint distribution of the eight-dimensional statistic summary only. It does not verify the full return process.

range_semantics: every 2.5-97.5% figure over the 20 replicates is an EMPIRICAL RANGE across 20 simulated pseudo-histories under a fixed known DGP. It is not a confidence interval for any real-market parameter.
